rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says most authorities classify al-Fātiḥa as Meccan, even counting it among the earliest revealed passages.
rows.anchor: بل من أوائل ما نزل

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وقتادة وأكثر الصحابة
rows.claim: Reports from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and most Companions support its Meccan origin.
rows.anchor: وهو المروي عن علي وابن عباس وقتادة وأكثر الصحابة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid calls the sūra Medinan; al-Ālūsī treats this solitary view as an error, noting it would mean years of prayer without al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد أنها مدنية( {[2]} ) ،  وقد تفرد بذلك حتى عد هفوة منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts say it descended both when prayer became obligatory in Mecca and when the qibla changed in Medina, or that parts are Meccan and Medinan; he calls the latter weak.
rows.anchor: وقيل نزلت بمكة حين فرضت الصلاة وبالمدينة لما حولت القبلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccan setting of 15:87 is often used to date al-Fātiḥa, but the argument depends on identifying the seven mathānī with it and on denying prior divine endowment.
rows.anchor: والأقوى الاستدلال بالنقل عن الصحابة الذين شاهدوا الوحي التنزيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others also explained the seven mathānī as the seven long sūras, weakening the dating argument from 15:87.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه قد صح أيضا عن ابن عباس وغيره تفسيرها بالسبع الطوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī notes that prior mention does not prove an event already occurred: 48:1 describes a future conquest in the past tense to assure its fulfillment.
rows.anchor: فهو قبل الفتح بسنين والتعبير بالماضي تحقيق للوقوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects repeated descent as an explanation reconciling reports: reports can validate an occurrence without causing it, and the alleged repeat lacks a sound rationale.
rows.anchor: وما قالوا في الجواب عن الاعتراض بأن النزول ظهور من عالم الغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūra may derive, with hamza, from the remnant of something, or without hamza from a building tier, an enclosing city wall, or elevation.
rows.anchor: والسورة مهموزة وغير مهموزة بإبدال

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha’s verse uses sūra for an elevated rank or station, supporting the sense of height.
rows.anchor: كما في قول النابغة : ألم تر أن الله أعطاك سورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He defines a sūra as Qurʾān containing an opening and a conclusion; another definition, an independent portion, distinguishes named units such as Āyat al-Kursī.
rows.anchor: قرآن يشتمل على ذي فاتحة وخاتمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fātiḥa was originally an adjective for the first part because it opens the whole; alternatively it is a verbal noun used for the object, as with al-Khātima.
rows.anchor: صفة جعلت إما لأول الشيء لكونه واسطة في فتح الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He finds an instrumental reading of fātiḥa unsuitable: the instrument need not share the action, and it could wrongly imply that the opening part is incidental.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا كالأول لقلة فاعلة في المصادر إلا أنه أولى

rows.speaker: أبو السعود
rows.claim: Abū al-Suʿūd explains the title’s first addition as the name of the named sūra and its second as possessive, meaning the opening of the Book.
rows.anchor: وهو مذهب بعض في كل

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان والسيرافي وجمع
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysān, al-Sīrāfī, and others treat the part-to-whole addition as partitive, with some grammarians extending that analysis to all such constructions.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن كيسان والسيرافي وجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fātiḥat al-Kitāb means the opening of the Qurʾān in its received order, not the first lesson taught or the first sūra revealed.
rows.anchor: لا لأنها يفتتح بها في التعليم وفي القراءة في الصلاة كما زعمه

rows.speaker: المرسي
rows.claim: Al-Mursī says it was named because it was the first sūra written on the Preserved Tablet; al-Ālūsī says this needs transmission and sequence of writing is uncertain.
rows.anchor: لأنها أول سورة كتبت في اللوح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umm al-Kitāb and Umm al-Qurʾān reflect its priority, like a mother preceding what follows, a banner leading an army, or its encompassing the Qurʾān’s aims.
rows.anchor: وسميت بذلك لأن الابتداء كتابة أو تلاوة أو نزولا على قول

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: The alleged prophetic prohibition on calling it Umm al-Kitāb has no basis; sound reports establish that title, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī also used it.
rows.anchor: بل قد ثبت في الصحاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says al-Fātiḥa gathers praise, worship, and promise or warning; these summarize the guidance sent through messengers and revealed books for worldly and final welfare.
rows.anchor: لأن بعثة الرسل وإنزال الكتب رحمة للعباد وإرشادا إلى ما يصلحهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praise appears in al-ḥamdu lillāh; worship is taught by its implied command, guidance-seeking, or the declaration of worship, while command entails prohibition.
rows.anchor: وأما التعبد فإما من الحمد لله لأنه للتعليم فيقدر أمر يفيده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He answers the Muʿtazilī objection that worship has no prior command: monotheism is worship’s foundation, and Muhammad’s prior charge to proclaim it suffices.
rows.anchor: بأن رأس العبادة التوحيد وفي الصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Promise and warning appear in the favored and the angered or astray, and in the Day of Recompense understood as reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: وأما الوعد والوعيد فمن قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī offers a second map: theoretical knowledge is covered through the Day of Judgment, practical conduct by worship and guidance, and human outcomes by the final verse.
rows.anchor: والأول مستفاد من أول السورة إلى قوله

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī’s threefold scheme may hint, in line with Muʿtazilī doctrine, that rational gratitude to the benefactor is obligatory; al-Ālūsī notes this implication.
rows.anchor: تلميحا إلى أن شكر المنعم واجب عقلا مراعاة لمذهب الاعتزال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A four-discipline scheme maps theology to Lordship and mercy, prophecy to those favored, and the afterlife to the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: علم الأصول ومعاقده معرفة الله تعالى وصفاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same scheme maps worship to practical law, reliance and guidance to ethics and spiritual progress, and the final verse to narratives, outcomes, and warning.
rows.anchor: علم الأخلاق وأجله الوصول إلى الحضرة الصمدانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says al-Fātiḥa equals two-thirds of the Qurʾān; al-Ālūsī disputes al-Shihāb’s reward-based explanation that the summary’s concision supplies a third.
rows.anchor: ومن العجب ما قيل هنا من أن ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Al-Dailamī’s report from Abū al-Dardāʾ says al-Fātiḥa outweighs the Qurʾān sevenfold on the scale; al-Ālūsī says its apparent reward claim challenges that explanation.
rows.anchor: الديلمي في الفردوس عن أبي الدرداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He suggests reconciling the virtue reports through increased later reward, differing circumstances, an inclusive use of equals, or Qurʾān meaning prayer as in 17:78.
rows.anchor: ويمكن التوفيق بين الخبرين وبه يزول الإشكال بأن الأول كان أولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed explanations for the title Umm al-Qurʾān include being the best sūra, having the sanctity of the whole Qurʾān, or being the believers’ refuge; he leaves these unendorsed.
rows.anchor: لأنها أفضل السور أو لأن حرمتها كحرمة القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other titles include al-Kanz, al-Wāfiya, al-Kāfiya, and al-Asās, associated with its gathered treasures, sufficiency, indivisibility in prayer, and status as Qurʾānic foundation.
rows.anchor: لما مر من اشتمالها على الجواهر المكنوزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names such as al-Ḥamd, al-Shukr, al-Duʿāʾ, Taʿlīm al-Masʾala, and al-Suʾāl describe its praise, gratitude, supplication, and instruction in asking.
rows.anchor: سورة الحمد وسورة الشكر وسورة الدعاء وسورة تعليم المسألة وسورة السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Munājāt and al-Tafwīḍ name its intimate address to God and the servant’s entrusting matters to Him.
rows.anchor: سورة المناجاة وسورة التفويض لأن العبد يناجي ربه بقوله إياك نعبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sound hadiths support its names al-Ruqya, al-Shifāʾ, and al-Shāfiya; it is also called al-Ṣalāh because it is required or recommended in prayer.
rows.anchor: الأحاديث الصحيحة مشعرة بذلك والتاسع عشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the sūra al-Ṣalāh is supported by the report “I divided the prayer”; prayer may stand for the sūra by whole-part relation or convention.
rows.anchor: قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nūr refers to its prominence, its illumination of hearts, or its embodiment of Qurʾānic meaning; al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm is another title.
rows.anchor: النور لظهورها بكثرة استعمالها أو لتنويرها القلوب لجلالة قدرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is the seven mathānī by agreement on seven verses; disputes over counting the basmala or “those You favored” are governed by transmitted reports.
rows.anchor: باتفاق وما رأينا مشاركا لها سوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathānī may refer to repeated recitation, repetition with another sūra, two revelation occasions, its combination of praise and prayer, or God’s response to each verse.
rows.anchor: أو المراد المتعارف الأغلب من الصلاة فلا ترد الركعة الواحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other derivations connect mathānī to praise of God or its reciter, or to God’s special bestowal of it on this community.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون من الثناء لما فيها من الثناء على الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dividing the Qurʾān into sūras energizes readers, makes each memorized unit feel complete, and establishes each sūra as an independent sign and miracle.
rows.anchor: أن يكون أنشط للقارئ وأبعث على التحصيل كالمسافر إذا قطع ميلا

rows.speaker: أبو بكر التونسي
rows.claim: Abū Bakr al-Tūnisī transmits a consensus that God opened every revealed book with the basmala; another report calls it the opening of every book.
rows.anchor: إجماع علماء كل ملة على أن الله تعالى افتتح كل كتاب بها

rows.speaker: السيوطي عن السرميني
rows.claim: Al-Suyūṭī, citing al-Sarmīnī, reports “the basmala is the opening of every book”; al-Ālūsī cautions that the transmission is the reporter’s responsibility.
rows.anchor: والعهدة عليه : بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم فاتحة كل كتاب

rows.speaker: السرميني
rows.claim: Al-Sarmīnī argues the Qurʾānic basmala is unique, citing the staged change from “in Your name” to “in God’s name,” then “the Merciful,” then the full formula.
rows.anchor: فأمر بكتابة بسم الله حتى نزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī replies that lack of an earlier command does not prove earlier absence, and only the Qurʾān’s Arabic wording and arrangement may be distinctive.
rows.anchor: وأن المختص بالقرآن اللفظ العربي بهذا الترتيب والكتب السماوية بأسرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Outside the sūra context of 27:30, scholars held ten positions: from nowhere a Qurʾānic verse to a verse or verse-part in all or selected sūras.
rows.anchor: اختلف الناس في البسملة في غير النمل إذ هي فيها بعض آية بالاتفاق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن المبارك وأهل مكة وأهل الكوفة وغالب أصحاب الشافعي والإمامية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Mubārak, Meccan and most Kufan readers, most Shāfiʿīs, and Imāmīs hold it is a verse in every sūra except al-Tawba.
rows.anchor: فابن عباس وابن المبارك وأهل مكة

rows.speaker: بعض الشافعية وحمزة
rows.claim: Some Shāfiʿīs and Ḥamza, with a view attributed to Aḥmad, count the basmala as a verse of al-Fātiḥa alone.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الشافعية وحمزة ونسب للإمام أحمد بالثالث

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة ومالك والأوزاعي وأبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: The Medinese, Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb hold it is a separate verse revealed to mark sūra openings; al-Ālūsī calls this the common Hanafi doctrine.
rows.anchor: وأهل المدينة ومنهم مالك والشام ومنهم الأوزاعي والبصرة ومنهم أبو عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the Hanafi position treats the basmala as an independent Qurʾānic verse, not part of al-Fātiḥa, while many Hanafis require its recitation in prayer.
rows.anchor: الصحيح من مذهبنا أن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم آية مستقلة وهي من القرآن

rows.speaker: الزيلعي والزهيدي وابن وهبان
rows.claim: Al-Zaylaʿī and al-Zāhidī report the sound Hanafi view as obligation, including each rakʿa with obligatory recitation; Ibn Wahbān prescribes prostration for forgetful omission.
rows.anchor: أن الأصح أنها واجبة ، وذكر الزاهدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī endorses the cautious view that omitting the basmala warrants the forgetfulness prostration, against Qāḍīkhān and the author of al-Khulāṣa.
rows.anchor: وهو الأحوط وبه أقول خلافا لقاضيخان

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: A report attributed to Umm Salama has the Prophet count the basmala as al-Fātiḥa’s first verse; al-Ālūsī questions the chain because Abū Mulayka’s hearing from her is unestablished.
rows.anchor: روى الشافعي عن ابن جريج عن أبي مليكة عن أم سلمة أنها قالت

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد وأحمد وأبو داود
rows.claim: They transmit Umm Salama’s report that the Prophet paused verse by verse, beginning with the basmala; al-Ālūsī says this proves its Qurʾānic status, not its membership in al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقطع قراءته آية آية بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: ابن خزيمة والحاكم
rows.claim: Their version has the Prophet count the basmala as a verse while reciting in prayer; al-Ālūsī reads it as the first Qurʾānic verse, not necessarily al-Fātiḥa’s.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قرأ في الصلاة بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم فعدها آية

rows.speaker: الدارقطني
rows.claim: Al-Dāraquṭnī’s version says the Prophet counted the basmala but did not pause after “those You favored”; al-Ālūsī says it is not explicit that it belongs to al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: والدارقطني بلفظ : «كان يقرأ بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report from Abū Hurayra says the seven verses of al-Fātiḥa begin with the basmala; al-Ālūsī reads the wording as counting seven al-Ḥamd verses and separately affirming the basmala as Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: فاتحة الكتاب سبع آيات أولاهن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Al-Dāraquṭnī’s report urges reciting the basmala before al-Ḥamd and calls it one of its verses; al-Ālūsī offers a figurative reading that preserves seven verses without it.
rows.anchor: إذا قرأتم الحمد فاقرءوا بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم إنها أم القرآن

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: In the sound Muslim report, God divides prayer between Himself and the servant; the three verses before the central pair and three after total seven without the basmala.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the Muslim version over al-Thaʿlabī’s and rejects readings that make the division merely semantic or mean half the prayer; it does not deny the basmala is Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: ولا شك أن هذه الرواية أصح من رواية الثعلبي ولا أقدم ثعلبياً على مسلم

rows.speaker: أبو ميسرة
rows.claim: An author-cited report from Abū Maysara says the Prophet first heard the call in Mecca, then recited al-Fātiḥa; al-Ālūsī says it would strongly prove Meccan origin if sound.
rows.anchor: عن أبي ميسرة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان إذا برز سمع مناديا

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet asked Ubayy the Qurʾān’s greatest verse; Ubayy answered the basmala and the Prophet affirmed it, proving a verse but not its place in al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: ما أعظم آية في القرآن ؟ قال : بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī transmits Jābir’s report that the Prophet instructed him to say the basmala when beginning prayer; al-Ālūsī says it does not establish sūra-part status.
rows.anchor: جعفر بن محمد عن أبيه عن جابر بن عبد الله

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī attributes to ʿAlī the practice of beginning each sūra in prayer with the basmala and saying omission diminishes the prayer; al-Ālūsī does not accept this as proof of inclusion.
rows.anchor: عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه

rows.speaker: طلحة بن عبيد الله
rows.claim: A report attributed to Ṭalḥa says whoever leaves the basmala has left a verse of God’s Book; al-Ālūsī says such reports establish its Qurʾānic status only.
rows.anchor: عن طلحة بن عبيد الله قال

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet rebuked a worshipper for beginning al-Ḥamd without the basmala and called omission a broken prayer; al-Ālūsī questions its wording and evidentiary force.
rows.anchor: يا رجل قطعت على نفسك الصلاة أما علمت أن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: معاوية
rows.claim: Reports say Medinese objected when Muʿāwiya omitted the basmala and he repeated the prayer; al-Ālūsī says this could concern a missed obligatory act and does not prove inclusion.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أم القرآن ولم يقرأ البسملة فلما قضى صلاته ناداه المهاجرون

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī’s report says Muʿāwiya omitted both the basmala and transition takbīrs, then repeated prayer after objections; al-Ālūsī says this poses no difficulty for his view.
rows.anchor: لم يكبر عند الخفض إلى الركوع والسجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s central reply to al-Rāzī is that obligation, Qurʾānic writing, and being an independent verse do not entail that the basmala is part of al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: الصحيح من مذهبنا أن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم آية مستقلة وهي من القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command “read in your Lord’s name” does not prove the basmala is part of al-Fātiḥa; the verse’s context concerns reading itself, and obligation does not entail inclusion.
rows.anchor: واستدلاله في هذا المقام بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its appearance in Qurʾānic script is al-Rāzī’s strongest evidence that it is Qurʾān, but it still does not show that it is part of al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: فهو أقوى ما يستدل به على كون البسملة من القرآن وأما على أنها من الفاتحة فلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument from seven verses assumes that Abū Ḥanīfa’s count is wrong; al-Ālūsī says that premise is difficult to establish.
rows.anchor: كلام مولانا أبي حنيفة رحمه الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the claim that a prayer without the basmala is incomplete under the “every important matter” report: prayer begins with its required opening takbīr.
rows.anchor: لأن الفاتحة جزء من الصلاة المفتتحة بالتكبير المقارن للنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse about following earlier prophets does not establish a binding basmala formula for Muhammad or prove that formula’s membership in al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: لا أدري ما أقول فيه سوى أنه جهل بالتفسير وعدم اطلاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated Qurʾānic phrases in other sūras do not prove the basmala is a constituent verse there; the comparison with repeated refrains is invalid.
rows.anchor: كذلك قلنا : إن الكل منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that the Prophet wrote “in Your name, O God” before the full basmala helps show Qurʾānic status, but not al-Fātiḥa membership.
rows.anchor: روى أنه عليه السلام كان يكتب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the independent Qurʾānic basmala should be recited in prayer; Hanafis may require it, and caution favors the ruling.
rows.anchor: ولا ينبغي لمن وقف على الأحاديث أن يتوقف في قرآنيتها أو ينكر وجوب قراءتها

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that he heard no basmala from the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān; al-Ālūsī takes this as silent recitation, not omission.
rows.anchor: صليت خلف النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبي بكر وعمر وعثمان فلم أسمع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Prophet did not recite the basmala aloud; al-Ālūsī reconciles this with occasional audible recitation for instruction.
rows.anchor: فعن ابن عباس لم يجهر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بالبسملة حتى مات

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن المغفل
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mughafal recounts his father’s objection to audible basmala, saying the Prophet and first caliphs began aloud with al-Ḥamd; al-Ālūsī infers they concealed the basmala.
rows.anchor: إياك والحدث في الإسلام فقد صليت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī lists many authorities for silent basmala recitation, including Sufyān, Ibn al-Mubārak, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujāhid, and Aḥmad.
rows.anchor: وهو مذهب الثوري وابن المبارك وابن مسعود وابن الزبير وعمار بن ياسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the explicit sound evidence for audible recitation is limited; reports of occasional loud recitation can demonstrate that it is read without making it habitual.
rows.anchor: وأحاديث الجهر لم يصح منها سوى حديث ابن عباس الذي أخرجه الشافعي

rows.speaker: الدارقطني
rows.claim: Al-Dāraquṭnī reportedly concluded, when pressed to identify sound evidence for audible basmala, that no report on the matter is sound.
rows.anchor: لم يصح في الجهر حديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conflicting Anas reports should be weighed by their chains; al-Ālūsī rejects accusing Anas of lying to protect an allegation about Umayyad pressure.
rows.anchor: ما يوافقنا إذ هو على شرط الشيخين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī’s six arguments for loud recitation fail: membership would not require identical volume, praise may be quiet, and reports and inferred commands are inconclusive.
rows.anchor: ذكر ست حجج لإثبات الجهر هي أخفى من العدم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī favors the bāʾ of accompaniment: blessing and reverence are readily understood, and accompaniment suggests God’s name pervades the whole act.
rows.anchor: وما يدل عليه كلام الزمخشري أرجحية الثاني

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī’s reading makes the bāʾ instrumental or one of seeking help; al-Ālūsī ultimately prefers this interpretation.
rows.anchor: فالذي يشعر به كلام البيضاوي أرجحية الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attachment, superiority, redundancy, and oath are also proposed for the bāʾ, but al-Ālūsī rejects these readings.
rows.anchor: والأربعة الأخيرة ليست بشيء وإن استؤنس لبعض ببعض الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers seeking divine aid because it expresses humility, denies independent human power, and anticipates “You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help.”
rows.anchor: بل يكاد أن تكون متعينة إذ فيها من الأدب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instrumental sense also fits 96:1 as a response to the Prophet’s “I am not a reader,” and echoes the command to seek God’s help.
rows.anchor: ولأنه كالمتعين في قوله

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr supplies an implied “I recite,” the specific act of the person uttering the basmala; al-Ālūsī finds this broad and contextually apt.
rows.anchor: فذهب الإمام ابن جرير إلى

rows.speaker: الفراء وابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ, with a view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, supplies an imperative addressed to people, urging them to begin in God’s name.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس لأنه تعالى قدم التسمية

rows.speaker: النحويون
rows.claim: Grammarians supply a general “I begin”; they argue it suits every basmala, but al-Ālūsī says it fails to convey that the entire recitation is aided by God’s name.
rows.anchor: وذهب النحويون إلى تقديره عاما نحو أبتدئ وأيد بوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers Ibn Jarīr’s specific verb because it makes the whole recitation occur with divine aid; the implied generic beginning adds little.
rows.anchor: وما ذهب إليه الإمام أمس وأخص بالمقصود وأتم شمولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An implied verbal noun such as “my beginning” adds an extra omitted predicate and loses the ongoing force of a finite verb.
rows.anchor: وذهب البعض إلى تقدير ابتدائي مثلا وفيه زيادة إضمار

rows.speaker: ابن عربي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabī reads the phrase’s implied predicate as the beginning and emergence of the cosmos through the divine names, an allusive reading beyond ordinary syntax.
rows.anchor: وجعل الشيخ الأكبر قدس سره هذا الجار خبر مبتدأ مضمر هو ابتداء العالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī favors placing the implied act before the basmala: God’s name precedes it in rank, and the order suggests beginning through divine aid.
rows.anchor: أن تقدير المتعلق هنا مؤخرا أحرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects a delayed implied verb because its placement fragments the construction or makes mercy seem to cause a reading that already occurred.
rows.anchor: وأما بعد التمام فيظهر نقص دقيق لأن في الجملة تعليق الحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prepositional phrase is “stable” under one terminology because its governing word is omitted; definitions of stable and non-stable adverbials vary by convention.
rows.anchor: وحيث لا مشاحة فيه اختار الأول فيكون الظرف هنا مستقرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ is kasra-marked despite the preference for light vowels on isolated particles: its prepositional function and genitive effect distinguish it.
rows.anchor: كسرت الباء في البسملة تعليما

rows.speaker: ابن الفارض
rows.claim: Ibn al-Fāriḍ’s verse makes the bāʾ’s kasra a sign of servile humility that is raised by divine generosity, not by human contrivance.
rows.anchor: سيدي عمر بن الفارض قدس الله تعالى سره

rows.speaker: الشبلي وابن عربي
rows.claim: Al-Shiblī identifies himself with the dot under bāʾ, and Ibn ʿArabī makes that dot a reminder of the heart and the secret of servanthood.
rows.anchor: وقال سيدي الشيخ الأكبر قدس سره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s allusion makes alif signify the divine essence and bāʾ its manifested attributes; its genitive kasra signifies lowered humility and mercy’s priority.
rows.anchor: والباء إما إشارة إلى صفاته التي أظهرتها نقطة الكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He links the basmala’s bāʾ to Muḥammad’s merciful reality and cites 21:107 and 9:128; the basmala’s opening then signals the Prophet’s mercy and mission.
rows.anchor: ولكون الغالب عليه الصلاة والسلام صفة الرحمة لا سيما على مؤمني الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He associates the missing basmala in al-Tawba with that sūra’s manifest severity, while claiming a concealed allusion to the Prophetic reality remains.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الجلال في سورة براءة ظاهرا ترك الإشارة بالبسملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Basrans derive ism from sumūw, “height,” with a deleted wāw; its function is to raise what is named from obscurity into recognition.
rows.anchor: وأصله سمو حذفت الواو تخفيفا لكثرة الاستعمال

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kufans derive ism from wasm, “mark,” and posit a compensatory hamza; al-Ālūsī rejects this as unsupported and prefers the Basran derivation.
rows.anchor: وقال الكوفيون : هو من السمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī records eighteen dialect forms for ism, including sim, sumā, and samāʾ, using inflected forms such as asāmī and summiyy to support the Basran root.
rows.anchor: أوصلها البعض إلى ثماني عشرة

rows.speaker: الأشاعرة والمعتزلة
rows.claim: Ashʿarīs say the name is the named, whereas Muʿtazilīs say it is other than the named; al-Ālūsī argues the dispute confuses essence with verbal designation.
rows.anchor: طال التشاجر في أن الاسم هل هو عين المسمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues that “glorify the name of your Lord” and “names you invented” can use name for the divine essence or idols, not merely their words.
rows.anchor: في المعروف إنما يتوجه إلى الذات الأقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He distinguishes God’s eternal names in eternal speech from later names used of Him; the former follow the dispute about divine speech, while created designations are other than God.
rows.anchor: قديم وهو ما سمى الله تعالى به نفسه في كلامه القديم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says objections that identity would multiply or change the named apply only to names as created expressions, not names used for the essence.
rows.anchor: والكل غير وارد إلا على تقدير القول بالعينية بناء على القسم الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take ism here as God’s essence because help cannot be sought through a bare word and none of the ninety-nine names is literally “name”; al-Ālūsī distinguishes constructions with bi-
rows.anchor: لأن الاستعانة بالألفاظ مجردها مما لا معنى لها وليس في التسعة والتسعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others say seeking blessing applies to a name even if seeking help applies to the named essence; they cite the distinction between swearing and auspicious invocation.
rows.anchor: وقال غير واحد سلمنا أن الاستعانة لا تكون إلا بالذات إلا أن التبرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The written basmala omits the alif of ism; explanations include frequent usage, the bāʾ replacing the initial hamza, and whether the governing word is stated.
rows.anchor: ولم تكتب همزة الوصل مع أن الأصل في كل كلمة أن ترسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī treats the Uthmānic spelling’s hidden alif as an allusion to the fullness of the bāʾ-sīn-mīm connection and universal mercy.
rows.anchor: والقريب من الفهم أن الهمزة إنما حذفت في الخط ليكون اتصال السين بالباء

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet instructed Muʿāwiya in calligraphy, including elongating the bāʾ, separating the sīns, and shaping the mīm; ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz gave similar advice.
rows.anchor: ألق الدواة وحرف القلم وانصب الباء وفرق السين ولا تعور الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Authorities derive Allāh either from al-ilāh or ilāh with hamza loss and compensatory alif-lām; Ibn Mālik instead argues for a distinct root and original proper name.
rows.anchor: على الأظهر وعوض عنها الألف واللام

rows.speaker: السيد السند والسعد والرضي
rows.claim: Al-Sayyid, al-Saʿd, and al-Raḍī differ on whether al-ilāh is generic or already exclusive, and whether Allāh became a proper name through deletion or assimilation.
rows.anchor: السيد السند : هما علم لذاته

rows.speaker: ابن مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Mālik denies that Allāh derives from al-ilāh, arguing their forms and meanings differ and that deletion or hamza transfer lacks a sound morphological parallel.
rows.anchor: وادعى ابن مالك أن الله من الأعلام التي قارن وضعها أل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proposed roots for Allāh include worship, bewilderment, finding refuge, seeking, and a calf’s attachment to its mother; al-Ālūsī weighs these as conjectural alternatives.
rows.anchor: واشتقاقه من أله كعبد إلاهة كعبادة وألوهة كعبودة

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s verse uses lāh as a divine designation, supporting the proposal that Allāh comes from a root meaning to be exalted or veiled.
rows.anchor: يشهدها لاهه الكبار

rows.speaker: البلخي
rows.claim: Al-Balkhī says Allāh is an Arabized Hebrew or Syriac word meaning powerful; al-Ālūsī rejects this without evidence and notes that Arabic morphology weighs against it.
rows.anchor: وزعم البلخي أنه ليس بعربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī favors Allāh as an Arabic proper name for the essence encompassing every attribute, following major theologians and the Naqshbandī tradition.
rows.anchor: فالذي أرتضيه لا عن تقليد أن هذا الاسم الأعظم موضوع للذات الجامعة

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī says Allāh began as an adjective but became proper through exclusive use; al-Ālūsī rejects his arguments from description, the heavenly predicate, and derivation.
rows.anchor: فاختار أنه وصف في أصله لكنه لما غلب عليه بحيث لا يستعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exclusive declaration “no god but God” supports a proper name: an adjective or generic noun would not itself prevent sharing, even if conventionally reserved.
rows.anchor: لو كان وصفا لم تكن الكلمة توحيدا مثل لا إله إلا الرحمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is emphatic after fatḥa or ḍamma according to common recitation practice; deletion of the alif is reported in pause, but retention is more eloquent.
rows.anchor: وتفخيم اللام من هذا الاسم الكريم إذا انفتح ما قبله أو انضم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ reports dropping Allāh’s alif; al-Taysīr confines it to pause, and some jurists call it erroneous enough to invalidate prayer or an explicit oath.
rows.anchor: والأفصح الإثبات حتى قال بعضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī points readers to Ibn ʿArabī’s extensive mystical treatment of the word’s letters, hidden and audible alif, and opening and ending structure.
rows.anchor: وأتى بالعجب العجاب ، وفي ظهور الألف تارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conventional analysis makes al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm intensive adjectives from rahima, sometimes positing transfer to intransitive rahuma; al-Ālūsī disputes this derivation.
rows.anchor: المشهور أنهما صفتان مشبهتان بنيتا لإفادة المبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interpreters explain divine mercy as its effect, the will to do good, a king’s compassion by analogy, or a metaphorical attribute; some call it a revealed technical sense.
rows.anchor: إما على طريقة المجاز المرسل بذكر لفظ السبب وإرادة المسبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects metaphorical reduction: mercy is truly God’s attribute in a manner befitting Him, without likening it to created emotion or specifying its modality.
rows.anchor: أو بتركه كذلك وإثباتها له حقيقة بالمعنى اللائق

rows.speaker: السكوني والأشعري
rows.claim: Al-Sakūnī condemns interpreting mercy metaphorically as an Muʿtazilī tendency; al-Ālūsī says al-Ashʿarī’s final position follows affirmation without asking how.
rows.anchor: قد نطق الإمام السكوني في كتابه

rows.speaker: الأشعري
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says reports that al-Ashʿarī interpreted mercy are either unestablished or superseded by the creed in his later al-Ibāna.
rows.anchor: إذا سئل أعطى والرحيم إذا لم يسئل غضب

rows.speaker: الراغب وابن المبارك
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib says raḥīm marks frequent action and raḥmān frequent, repeated action; Ibn al-Mubārak says the Merciful gives when asked, while the Compassionate is angered if not asked.
rows.anchor: ابن المبارك الرحمن : إذا سئل أعطى

rows.speaker: الجويني
rows.claim: Al-Juwaynī treats the two names as equal in force, distinguishing repeated abundance in raḥmān from enduring action in raḥīm.
rows.anchor: وفرق بعضهم بينهما بأن الرحمة دال على الصفة القائمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some distinguish raḥmān as the attribute of mercy and raḥīm as its relation to recipients, citing human use of raḥīm in 9:117 and 33:43 but not raḥmān.
rows.anchor: وفرق بعضهم بينهما بأن الرحمة دال على الصفة القائمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī challenges the rule that greater form means greater intensity and disputes whether raḥmān is more abundant, more enduring, or simply equal to raḥīm.
rows.anchor: وأما سادسا فلأن كون الرحمن أبلغ من الرحيم غير مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One distinction makes raḥmān’s worldly mercy encompass believers and unbelievers and raḥīm’s afterlife mercy favor believers; al-Ālūsī questions the allocation and its assumptions.
rows.anchor: فعلى الأول قيل يا رحمن الدنيا لأنه يعم المؤمن والكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s intercession for all people at the gathering and reports of punishment relief complicate claims that afterlife mercy reaches only believers.
rows.anchor: لما كان المقصود تعليم وجه التيمن بأسمائه الحسنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proposed reasons for placing al-Raḥmān first include its encompassing major blessings, al-Raḥīm completing lesser ones, or preserving verse-end rhyme; al-Ālūsī rejects rhyme alone.
rows.anchor: أو للمحافظة على رؤوس الآي

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī’s ordering moves from God’s universal outpouring of existence to each creature’s particular share and perfection; al-Ālūsī questions the distinction.
rows.anchor: وللعلماء في هذا الترتيب كلام كثير

rows.speaker: ابن هشام وابن خروف
rows.claim: Ibn Hishām treats al-Raḥmān as a substitute, not adjective, with al-Raḥīm modifying it; Ibn Khurūf calls it a dominant adjective.
rows.anchor: وأن استفاضة إضافته نحو رحمن الدنيا تنافيه فتأمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s allusive reading makes al-Raḥīm an epithet of Muḥammad from 9:128: Adam bears the names, while Muḥammad bears their meanings and completes creation.
rows.anchor: وعندي من باب الإشارة أن تأخير الرحيم لأنه صفة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن الحاجب والزمخشري والرضي وابن مالك والبيضاوي والسعد
rows.claim: Grammarians dispute whether raḥmān declines: most prefer diptote treatment by analogy with the predominant faʿlā feminine pattern, while al-Saʿd allows both.
rows.anchor: واختلف فيما لزم تذكيره كلحيان بمعنى كبير اللحية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Banū Ḥanīfa called Musaylima “the Merciful of Yamāma”; al-Ālūsī treats this as blasphemous excess, not evidence that the sacred name is ordinarily shared.
rows.anchor: وأنت غيث الورى لا زلت رحمانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basmala opens God’s discourse because it summarizes what follows and is a profound blessing; analyzing even its brief wording draws on many disciplines.
rows.anchor: لأنها إجمال ما بعدها وهي آية عظيمة ونعمة للعارف جسيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its study ranges from syntax, morphology, rhetoric, language, and script to logic, theology, jurisprudence, hadith method, ethics, and esoteric knowledge.
rows.anchor: إذا أراد أن يبحث عن الباء من حيث إنها حرف جر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī finds layered triads in its articulation, omitted letters, written and spoken forms, word classes, genitives, divine names, grammatical roles, and connections.
rows.anchor: وانظر لم اشتملت حروفها على الطبائع الأربع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reason for opening with the basmala is to teach people how to begin: invoking God declares dependence on His power in every undertaking.
rows.anchor: لتعليم العباد إذا بدءوا بأمر كيف يبدءون

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra transmits the Prophet’s maxim that an important matter begun without God’s name is incomplete; al-Ālūsī interprets it broadly to include trivial matters.
rows.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لا يبدأ فيه ببسم الله فهو أبتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī takes dhū bāl as comprehensive—anything that enters the mind—rather than restricting it to dignified matters, since God’s aid matters in small acts too.
rows.anchor: أي كل أمر يخطر بالبال جليلا كان أو حقيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports urge asking God even for a sandal strap, and God tells Moses to ask for salt and a shoe strap; these support invocation in minor needs.
rows.anchor: يا موسى سلني حتى ملح قدرك وشراك نعلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reciting the basmala over forbidden acts is itself forbidden without being disbelief according to the sound view; over disliked acts it is disliked, unless contempt makes it disbelief.
rows.anchor: التسمية على الحرام والمكروه مما لا ينبغي بل هي حرام في الحرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The maxim’s variants include beginning with praise, “praise of God,” or another remembrance, and incomplete versus severed; al-Ālūsī calls it unstable in wording and chain but strengthened in meaning.
rows.anchor: وقد اضطرب الحديث هنا فوقع في بعض الروايات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī reconciles variants by taking the intended opening as remembrance that manifests divine perfection; matters may be outwardly complete yet deficient in meaning without it.
rows.anchor: واستحسن فيه أن روايتي البسملة والحمدلة تعارضتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it fittingly precedes the comprehensive praise that follows.
rows.anchor: ولما افتتح سبحانه وتعالى كتابة البسملة وهي نوع من الحمد ناسب
